use: The everyday spoken zero; rei is the formal version used in weather, scores and announcements.

example.ja: バッテリーもうゼロだよ。

examplePolite.ja: バッテリーがもうゼロです。
examplePolite.english: My battery is already at zero.

notes: Rei (零) is heard in temperatures like rei do (0 degrees). In phone numbers people say zero or maru.

use: For counting, prices, times and maths; one thing is hitotsu and one person is hitori.

examplePolite.romaji: Ichi kara juu made kazoete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一から十まで数えてください。
examplePolite.english: Please count from one to ten.

notes: Shortens to i- with a doubled sound before many counters: ikko, issai, ippun, ippon.

example.english: The room's on the second floor.

examplePolite.english: The room is on the second floor.

notes: Stretched to nii when reading out phone numbers so it isn't missed.

examplePolite.english: Shall we meet at three?

notes: Softens the next sound: sanbyaku, sanzen, sanbon, sanbai. Not the name suffix -san.

use: The default four; shi appears in shigatsu (April) and when counting ichi, ni, san, shi aloud.

examplePolite.romaji: Yonban no basu ni notte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 四番のバスに乗ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please take the number four bus.

notes: Shi also sounds like 'death', so it's avoided. Four o'clock is yoji and four people is yonin.

example.english: I'll be there in five minutes.

examplePolite.english: I'll arrive in five minutes.

notes: Stretched to goo when reading out phone numbers.

examplePolite.english: I got up at six.

notes: Shortens to rop- before h and p sounds: roppyaku, roppon, roppun.

use: The safe default seven; shichi is standard in shichigatsu (July) and common in shichiji (7 o'clock).

example.romaji: Nanasai no musume ga iru yo.

examplePolite.english: I have a seven-year-old daughter.

notes: Shichi is easy to mishear as ichi, which is why people switch to nana.

examplePolite.english: I'll call you at eight.

notes: Shortens to hap- or has- before many counters: happyaku, hassen, happon, hassai.

use: The default nine; 9 o'clock is kuji and September is kugatsu.

example.romaji: Shiai wa kyuu tai ichi datta.
example.english: The game finished nine to one.

examplePolite.romaji: Shiai wa kyuu tai ichi deshita.
examplePolite.english: The game finished nine to one.

notes: Not the same word as kyuu ni (suddenly).

examplePolite.english: I'm ten yen short.

notes: Shortens to jup- or jus- before many counters: juppun, juppon, jussai, jukkai.

name: Numbers 11-19
formation: juu + digit: juuichi, juuni, juusan, juuyon, juugo, juuroku, juunana, juuhachi, juukyuu
use: Teens are ten plus the digit, with the same yon, nana and kyuu choices as the digits.

example.ja: 十一時まで開いてるよ。

examplePolite.ja: 十一時まで開いています。
examplePolite.english: It's open until eleven.

notes: Juuyon is the usual 14; juushichi and juunana are both common for 17.

name: Tens 20-99
formation: digit + juu (+ digit): nijuu, sanjuu, yonjuu, gojuu, rokujuu, nanajuu, hachijuu, kyuujuu; nijuugo = 25
english: twenty (and the tens: digit times ten)
use: Tens put the digit before juu, and use yon, nana and kyuu.

examplePolite.english: I'm already twenty-five.

notes: Age 20 is hatachi, not nijussai.

use: Hyaku alone means one hundred; no ichi in front.

example.english: You can get it for a hundred yen.

examplePolite.english: You can buy it for a hundred yen.

notes: Changes after 3, 6 and 8: sanbyaku, roppyaku, happyaku. A hyaku en shoppu is a 100-yen shop.

examplePolite.english: This is three hundred yen.

notes: Not sanhyaku: h turns to b after san. Nanbyaku (how many hundred) changes the same way.

example.english: The ticket was six hundred yen.

examplePolite.english: The ticket was six hundred yen.

notes: Not rokuhyaku: roku shortens to rop- and h becomes p.

example.romaji: Ranchi, happyaku en de yasui ne.
example.ja: ランチ、八百円で安いね。
example.english: Lunch is cheap at eight hundred yen.

examplePolite.romaji: Ranchi wa happyaku en de yasui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ランチは八百円で安いですね。
examplePolite.english: Lunch is cheap at eight hundred yen.

notes: Not hachihyaku: hachi shortens to hap- and h becomes p.

use: Sen alone means one thousand; issen is only heard inside issenman (ten million).

examplePolite.ja: 千円貸してくれませんか。
examplePolite.english: Could you lend me a thousand yen?

notes: Changes after 3 and 8: sanzen, hassen. How many thousand is nanzen.

examplePolite.english: Will three thousand yen be enough?

notes: Not sansen: s turns to z after san.

example.ja: ホテル、八千円だったよ。
example.english: The hotel was eight thousand yen.

examplePolite.ja: ホテルは八千円でした。
examplePolite.english: The hotel was eight thousand yen.

notes: Not hachisen. Rokusen (6,000) stays regular.
